title: Praxis Audiology (5343) — 200 Source Questions + 100 Independent Practice Questions + 200 Guided Review
description: Contains 200 original source questions, 100 assistant-authored independent practice questions, and 200 source-derived guided-review activities. The assistant audit found 252 distinct independent content kernels. Two independently authored 100-question diagnostic batches linked to a 12-chapter learning library, targeted skill practice, and an optional 120-question timed simulation. The official 5343 test currently has 120 selected-response questions in 120 minutes; AlloFlow practice is not an official form or score.
contentReview: Assistant audit completed: 300 independent-practice items contain 252 distinct content kernels and 48 parallel variants under the normalized test. 200 additional activities are guided reasoning transformations, not independent exam questions. The 500-distinct-question target is not met.
disclaimer: Independent preparation material. Not affiliated with or endorsed by ETS or ASHA. The official Praxis Audiology (5343) test currently has 120 selected-response questions in 120 minutes; the 100-item diagnostic batches are not official-length forms. Practice results are not official or scaled Praxis scores, pass predictions, credentials, clinical evaluations, diagnoses, medical or vestibular decisions, device fittings, treatment, legal advice, or substitutes for qualified supervision, urgent medical care, and current federal, state, local, licensure, certification, educational, health-care, privacy, consent, emergency, and reporting requirements.

items.prompt: What is the primary function of the ossicular chain?
choices: They transform acoustic energy and improve impedance matching between ear-canal air and cochlear fluid.
They generate electrical action potentials directly and send them along the eighth nerve to the brainstem.
They decode complex speech phonology and extract word meaning before signals reach the auditory cortex.
They pump ions across cochlear membranes to equalize endolymph and perilymph chemical concentrations.
items.rationale: The middle-ear system transfers energy from air to fluid through area and lever relationships while preserving a usable acoustic signal.
choiceRationales: Correct. The middle-ear system transfers energy from air to fluid through area and lever relationships while preserving a usable acoustic signal.
Neural action potentials originate at the inner hair cell and auditory-nerve synapse rather than inside the mechanical middle-ear ossicles.
Speech perception and meaning analysis take place across central auditory and language networks rather than in the ossicular chain.
The stria vascularis maintains cochlear fluid composition and endocochlear potential, whereas the ossicles transfer mechanical energy.

items.prompt: Which cochlear region responds most strongly to high-frequency sound?
choices: The apical end of the cochlea near the helicotrema.
The basal end of the cochlea near the oval window.
The air-filled middle-ear cavity behind the eardrum.
The primary auditory cortex prior to cochlear tuning.
items.rationale: Cochlear tonotopy places high-frequency maxima toward the base and low-frequency maxima toward the apex. This response best integrates audiologic evidence, the referral purpose, person and family priorities, safety, access, professional scope, and appropriate follow-up.
choiceRationales: The wider, more flexible apical membrane near the helicotrema responds maximally to low-frequency rather than high-frequency sounds.

Correct. Cochlear tonotopy places high-frequency maxima toward the base and low-frequency maxima toward the apex. This response best integrates audiologic evidence, the referral purpose, person and family priorities, safety, access, professional scope, and appropriate follow-up.
The middle-ear space transmits broad acoustic energy mechanically via the ossicles and does not perform tonotopic cochlear filtering.
Tonotopic frequency separation begins along the basilar membrane inside the cochlea before ascending signals reach auditory cortex.

items.prompt: What is the major role of outer hair cells?
choices: They contract the stapedius muscle reflexively to stiffen the ossicular chain during loud sound exposure.
They generate the resting endocochlear potential independently without contributions from the stria vascularis.
They provide active cochlear amplification and sharpen frequency selectivity along the basilar membrane.
They carry nearly all vestibular balance afferents from the semicircular canals into the central brainstem.
items.rationale: Outer hair-cell motility enhances basilar-membrane motion at low levels and contributes to sensitivity, compression, and sharp tuning.
choiceRationales: The stapedius is a middle-ear skeletal muscle innervated by the facial nerve rather than driven by cochlear outer hair cells.
The stria vascularis generates and maintains the positive endocochlear potential that powers hair-cell transduction in scala media.
Correct. Outer hair-cell motility enhances basilar-membrane motion at low levels and contributes to sensitivity, compression, and sharp tuning.
Vestibular hair cells in the otolith organs and semicircular canals—not cochlear outer hair cells—encode balance afferents.

items.prompt: What is the primary sensory role of inner hair cells?
choices: They serve as the main electromotile cochlear amplifier that sharpens mechanical basilar-membrane tuning.
They contract periodically during swallowing to open the Eustachian tube and ventilate the middle ear.
They regulate middle-ear static air pressure directly across changing ambient atmospheric altitudes.
They transduce cochlear motion into neural signals carried by most auditory-nerve afferent fibers.
items.rationale: Inner hair cells are the principal sensory receptors for hearing and synapse with most type I auditory-nerve fibers. This response best integrates audiologic evidence, the referral purpose, person and family priorities, safety, access, professional scope, and appropriate follow-up.
choiceRationales: Outer hair cells—not inner hair cells—provide the active mechanical amplification and sharp frequency tuning of the cochlea.
Tensor veli palatini and palatal muscles open the Eustachian tube during swallowing rather than cochlear sensory receptor cells.
Middle-ear pressure equalization depends on Eustachian-tube ventilation and mucosa, whereas inner hair cells perform sensory transduction.

Correct. Inner hair cells are the principal sensory receptors for hearing and synapse with most type I auditory-nerve fibers. This response best integrates audiologic evidence, the referral purpose, person and family priorities, safety, access, professional scope, and appropriate follow-up.

items.prompt: Which cranial nerve carries cochlear and vestibular information?
choices: The vestibulocochlear nerve, cranial nerve VIII.
The visual optic nerve, cranial nerve II.
The motor facial nerve, cranial nerve VII.
The tongue hypoglossal nerve, cranial nerve XII.
items.rationale: Cranial nerve VIII includes cochlear and vestibular divisions and carries sensory information toward the brainstem. This response best integrates audiologic evidence, the referral purpose, person and family priorities, safety, access, professional scope, and appropriate follow-up.
choiceRationales: Correct. Cranial nerve VIII includes cochlear and vestibular divisions and carries sensory information toward the brainstem. This response best integrates audiologic evidence, the referral purpose, person and family priorities, safety, access, professional scope, and appropriate follow-up.
Cranial nerve II carries visual information from retinal ganglion cells to the brain and conveys no auditory or vestibular input.
Cranial nerve VII supplies facial expression muscles, taste, and the stapedius muscle rather than carrying cochlear and vestibular afferents.
Cranial nerve XII innervates intrinsic and extrinsic tongue muscles for speech and swallowing rather than auditory or balance pathways.

items.prompt: A patient has a focal lesion above the cochlear nuclei yet retains some audibility for signals presented to either ear. Which neural organization best accounts for this finding?
choices: Above the cochlear nuclei, ascending auditory projections remain strictly ipsilateral through the cortex.
Ascending auditory projections become extensively bilateral above the cochlear nuclei.
The facial nerve regenerates bilateral sensory input whenever one central auditory pathway is damaged.
Vestibular projections replace the damaged cochlear signal before it reaches the auditory brainstem.
items.rationale: Above the cochlear nuclei, substantial crossing and bilateral ascending projections allow input from either ear to reach structures on both sides. This organization supports binaural processing and helps explain why one rostral central lesion seldom eliminates all audibility from one ear.
choiceRationales: Not the best answer. Central auditory projections do not remain confined to the stimulated side after the cochlear nuclei; multiple crossings distribute information to both sides of the ascending system.

Correct. Above the cochlear nuclei, substantial crossing and bilateral ascending projections allow input from either ear to reach structures on both sides. This organization supports binaural processing and helps explain why one rostral central lesion seldom eliminates all audibility from one ear.
Not the best answer. The facial nerve supplies the stapedius efferent limb and facial motor functions; it does not regenerate bilateral afferent auditory input after a central lesion.

Not the best answer. Vestibular and cochlear afferents share cranial nerve VIII proximally, but vestibular projections do not replace damaged auditory input or account for preserved cortical audibility.

items.prompt: Which equation relates sound-pressure ratios to decibels?
choices: Ten times the arithmetic pressure difference measured directly in linear pascals.
The squared ratio of the two sound pressures without applying any logarithmic scale.
Twenty times the base-10 logarithm of the ratio between the two sound pressures.
The acoustic frequency in hertz divided directly by the corresponding sound wavelength.
items.rationale: Sound pressure level uses 20 log10 of a pressure ratio because acoustic intensity is proportional to pressure squared. This response best integrates audiologic evidence, the referral purpose, person and family priorities, safety, access, professional scope, and appropriate follow-up.
choiceRationales: Decibels use a logarithmic ratio rather than a linear difference, and power ratios—not linear pascal differences—use a factor of ten.
Squaring a pressure ratio yields an intensity ratio, yet converting to decibels still requires taking the base-10 logarithm.

Correct. Sound pressure level uses 20 log10 of a pressure ratio because acoustic intensity is proportional to pressure squared. This response best integrates audiologic evidence, the referral purpose, person and family priorities, safety, access, professional scope, and appropriate follow-up.
Multiplying frequency by wavelength equals sound speed; dividing frequency by wavelength does not produce a decibel level.

items.prompt: In a free field, what happens to sound pressure level when distance from a point source doubles?
choices: Sound pressure level increases by about 6 dB.
Sound pressure level drops by exactly 20 dB.
Sound pressure level stays unchanged across distance.
Sound pressure level decreases by about 6 dB.
items.rationale: Under ideal free-field conditions, pressure halves when distance doubles, corresponding to an approximately 6 dB reduction.
choiceRationales: Moving farther from a point source spreads acoustic energy over a larger area, reducing rather than raising sound pressure level.
A 20 dB drop corresponds to a tenfold increase in distance under free-field conditions rather than simply doubling distance.
In a free field, spherical spreading attenuates sound inversely with distance, so level falls rather than staying constant.
Correct. Under ideal free-field conditions, pressure halves when distance doubles, corresponding to an approximately 6 dB reduction.

items.prompt: How are frequency, wavelength, and sound speed related?
choices: Wavelength decreases because wavelength equals the speed of sound divided by acoustic frequency.
Wavelength increases proportionally as frequency rises while acoustic propagation speed stays fixed.
Wavelength stays completely independent of frequency whenever sound travels through uniform room air.
The speed of sound drops toward zero as high-frequency tones oscillate more rapidly through air.
items.rationale: For a given medium, speed equals frequency times wavelength, so higher frequency has shorter wavelength. This response best integrates audiologic evidence, the referral purpose, person and family priorities, safety, access, professional scope, and appropriate follow-up.
choiceRationales: Correct. For a given medium, speed equals frequency times wavelength, so higher frequency has shorter wavelength. This response best integrates audiologic evidence, the referral purpose, person and family priorities, safety, access, professional scope, and appropriate follow-up.
Frequency and wavelength vary inversely at constant sound speed, so higher-frequency tones always have shorter wavelengths.
Because wavelength equals speed divided by frequency, altering frequency directly changes the spatial length of each wave cycle.
Acoustic propagation speed depends on the medium’s properties such as air temperature rather than falling as frequency rises.

items.prompt: Why are calibration and biological checks both needed?
choices: Daily listening checks satisfy acoustic output standards and replace annual electroacoustic audiometer calibration.
Calibration verifies traceable output, while routine checks catch interim equipment, transducer, or room faults.
Passing annual calibration guarantees stable transducer output so daily biological listening checks add no value.
Neither calibration nor routine listening checks are required whenever patient thresholds look clinically plausible.
items.rationale: Quality assurance combines scheduled calibration with routine inspection and checks so measurement problems are found before affecting clients.
choiceRationales: Biological checks detect gross distortions, static, or intermittent cords, yet they cannot measure traceable ANSI output precision.
Correct. Quality assurance combines scheduled calibration with routine inspection and checks so measurement problems are found before affecting clients.
Transducers can drop, cords fray, and rooms get noisy between annual visits, so routine checks protect daily test validity.
Plausible-looking thresholds can still be shifted by miscalibration or faulty earphones, making both safeguards clinically essential.

items.prompt: What does an auditory threshold represent?
choices: The most comfortable listening level at which everyday conversation feels effortless and clear to the listener.
The upper loudness discomfort level where acoustic signals begin to feel uncomfortably intense or painful.
The lowest signal level detected under defined test conditions using a specified response criterion.
The presentation level required to guarantee one hundred percent word recognition across noisy environments.
items.rationale: Threshold is an operational estimate influenced by procedure, criterion, attention, noise, transducer, and auditory status.
choiceRationales: Most comfortable loudness sits well above minimum audibility and describes preferred suprathreshold listening rather than detection threshold.
Loudness discomfort defines the top edge of the listener’s dynamic range rather than the softest detectable signal level.
Correct. Threshold is an operational estimate influenced by procedure, criterion, attention, noise, transducer, and auditory status.
Threshold estimates faint sound detection under specified rules rather than predicting perfect suprathreshold speech recognition in noise.

items.prompt: What is loudness recruitment in cochlear hearing loss?
choices: Conductive attenuation: uniform sound reduction caused by middle-ear fluid blocking acoustic transmission.
Binaural diplacusis: pitch mismatch in which one pure tone sounds different in frequency between ears.
Masking-level release: improved tone detection in noise created by an out-of-phase binaural masker.
Unusually rapid perceived-intensity growth once sounds exceed an elevated inner-ear threshold.
items.rationale: Recruitment is abnormally rapid loudness growth often associated with cochlear dysfunction and reduced dynamic range. This response best integrates audiologic evidence, the referral purpose, person and family priorities, safety, access, professional scope, and appropriate follow-up.
choiceRationales: Conductive attenuation reduces soft and loud sounds similarly without producing the compressed dynamic range typical of cochlear loss.
Perceiving the same frequency as different pitches between ears defines diplacusis rather than abnormal loudness growth.
Detecting a tone better due to binaural phase differences describes masking-level difference rather than cochlear loudness recruitment.

Correct. Recruitment is abnormally rapid loudness growth often associated with cochlear dysfunction and reduced dynamic range. This response best integrates audiologic evidence, the referral purpose, person and family priorities, safety, access, professional scope, and appropriate follow-up.

items.prompt: A 2000 Hz tone becomes less detectable when nearby noise activates overlapping cochlear filters, even though attention to the task is stable. Which mechanism best explains the threshold shift?
choices: Energetic masking from physical overlap between masker and target excitation.
Informational masking from uncertainty about which auditory object is the target.
Binaural summation from combining matching signals delivered to both ears.
Auditory adaptation from continued stimulation after the competing noise ends.
items.rationale: Energetic masking occurs when masker energy overlaps the auditory-filter excitation used to detect the target, reducing the target’s effective signal-to-masker relationship. The scenario holds attention stable and locates the interference in overlapping cochlear excitation rather than uncertainty or postexposure adaptation.
choiceRationales: Correct. The nearby masker activates overlapping auditory filters and reduces physical detectability of the target, which is the defining mechanism of energetic masking in this scenario.

Not the best answer. Informational masking reflects uncertainty, similarity, or difficulty selecting an auditory object beyond energetic overlap; the scenario instead specifies cochlear-filter interference with stable attention.
Not the best answer. Binaural summation can improve detection when related information is combined across ears and does not describe a nearby noise making this target less detectable.
Not the best answer. Adaptation concerns response change with continued stimulation or aftereffects and does not account for the simultaneous overlapping masker described here.

items.prompt: What does the critical-band concept describe?
choices: Every cochlear site responds with equal sensitivity across the entire audible frequency spectrum simultaneously.
The auditory system processes sound through frequency-selective filters of limited spectral bandwidth.
Auditory masking strength depends primarily on visual distraction rather than spectral proximity to the tone.
Critical bands reflect middle-ear stapedius muscle contractions that selectively dampen narrow tone ranges.
items.rationale: Auditory-filter bandwidth helps explain masking, frequency selectivity, and how noise energy influences detection. This response best integrates audiologic evidence, the referral purpose, person and family priorities, safety, access, professional scope, and appropriate follow-up.
choiceRationales: The basilar membrane is tonotopically tuned, so only noise falling near a tone’s auditory filter masks it efficiently.

Correct. Auditory-filter bandwidth helps explain masking, frequency selectivity, and how noise energy influences detection. This response best integrates audiologic evidence, the referral purpose, person and family priorities, safety, access, professional scope, and appropriate follow-up.
Energetic masking is governed strongly by spectral overlap inside the critical band rather than by visual attention alone.
The acoustic reflex stiffens middle-ear transmission broadly at low frequencies rather than creating cochlear frequency filters.

items.prompt: Which binaural cue is most useful for low-frequency localization?
choices: High-frequency spectral filtering cues created by the outer pinna.
Interaural sound-level differences created by strong head shadow.
Interaural timing and phase differences between the two ears.
Middle-ear tympanometric peak pressure measured across both canals.
items.rationale: Low-frequency localization relies strongly on timing information, while high-frequency localization relies more on level differences.
choiceRationales: Pinna spectral notches operate mainly at higher frequencies to resolve front–back and vertical elevation rather than low-frequency azimuth.
Low-frequency sound waves bend easily around the head, leaving minimal head-shadow level contrast compared with timing cues.
Correct. Low-frequency localization relies strongly on timing information, while high-frequency localization relies more on level differences.
Tympanometric peak pressure reflects middle-ear ventilation status and does not serve as a binaural spatial localization cue.

items.prompt: Which cue is especially important for high-frequency horizontal localization?
choices: Low-frequency bone-conduction occlusion in the ear canal.
Middle-ear stapedius acoustic reflex decay over time.
Resting cochlear endocochlear electrical voltage potential.
Interaural level differences produced by head shadow.
items.rationale: The head attenuates high-frequency sound reaching the far ear, creating useful interaural level differences. This response best integrates audiologic evidence, the referral purpose, person and family priorities, safety, access, professional scope, and appropriate follow-up.
choiceRationales: The occlusion effect enhances low-frequency bone-conducted sound in an enclosed canal rather than supporting high-frequency localization.
Acoustic reflex decay assesses retrocochlear adaptation of the stapedius reflex rather than binaural spatial hearing cues.
The endocochlear potential supplies electrical energy for cochlear hair-cell transduction rather than encoding horizontal sound location.

Correct. The head attenuates high-frequency sound reaching the far ear, creating useful interaural level differences. This response best integrates audiologic evidence, the referral purpose, person and family priorities, safety, access, professional scope, and appropriate follow-up.

items.prompt: Why can speech understanding in noise be poor despite near-normal pure-tone thresholds?
choices: Speech in noise also relies on suprathreshold processing, binaural cues, cognition, language, and room acoustics.
Normal pure-tone thresholds predict real-world listening accurately across reverberant and noisy classroom rooms.
Difficulty understanding speech in noise despite good quiet thresholds indicates deliberate nonorganic malingering.
Middle-ear static air pressure alone governs how clearly a listener separates target talkers from background noise.
items.rationale: Tone detection is not equivalent to complex communication; functional assessment should sample realistic listening demands.
choiceRationales: Correct. Tone detection is not equivalent to complex communication; functional assessment should sample realistic listening demands.
Quiet tone detection samples peripheral sensitivity only and often misses suprathreshold, binaural, reverberation, and cognitive listening limits.
Many genuine peripheral, neural, central, and acoustic factors impair speech in noise without implying nonorganic malingering.
Middle-ear pressure affects conductive transmission yet does not capture binaural release, temporal cues, or cognitive speech processing.

items.prompt: What develops during early auditory experience?
choices: Human central auditory maturation finishes before birth, leaving early postnatal listening experience largely secondary.
Auditory, speech, language, and neural systems develop through interacting biology, access, experience, and bonding.
Reduced early hearing access affects spoken vocabulary lists while leaving broader communication development untouched.
Timely early audiologic intervention eliminates individual developmental variability across all infants with hearing loss.
items.rationale: Early accessible communication and family-centered intervention can support development while outcomes remain shaped by many child and environmental factors.
choiceRationales: Central auditory pathways show robust postnatal plasticity driven by meaningful auditory and language access during early childhood.
Correct. Early accessible communication and family-centered intervention can support development while outcomes remain shaped by many child and environmental factors.
Hearing access interacts with phonology, syntax, pragmatics, literacy, and social-emotional connection far beyond isolated spoken vocabulary.
Early access strongly improves outcomes yet interacts with etiology, family language, comorbidities, and ongoing individual diversity.

items.prompt: Which pattern is typical of age-related sensorineural hearing change?
choices: Acute unilateral conductive hearing loss defined by gradual bilateral high-frequency threshold decline.
Clinically normal hearing requiring no counseling because low-frequency pure-tone thresholds remain strong.
Presbycusis, interpreted alongside noise, medical, genetic, cognitive, and personal listening history.
A purely peripheral vestibular balance disorder that carries no implications for speech communication.
items.rationale: Age-related change often affects high frequencies and speech understanding, but differential evaluation considers multiple lifetime contributors.
choiceRationales: Presbycusis is typically bilateral, gradual, and sensorineural rather than an acute one-sided conductive outer- or middle-ear problem.
High-frequency loss impairs consonant perception and speech in noise substantially even when low frequencies stay near normal.
Correct. Age-related change often affects high frequencies and speech understanding, but differential evaluation considers multiple lifetime contributors.
Age-related sensorineural hearing change directly impacts speech communication and listening effort rather than being purely vestibular.

items.prompt: What is temporal resolution in auditory processing?
choices: The peripheral sensitivity required to detect faint high-frequency pure tones in quiet booths.
The mechanical peak static compliance measured across the tympanic membrane during tympanometry.
The visual cortex capacity to resolve fine spatial detail when reading speechreading cues.
The perceptual ability to detect rapid timing changes and brief silent gaps over time.
items.rationale: Temporal resolution contributes to processing rapidly changing speech and environmental sounds and is distinct from threshold sensitivity.
choiceRationales: High-frequency threshold sensitivity reflects spectral audibility rather than how quickly the auditory system tracks rapid timing shifts.
Static acoustic admittance measures middle-ear mobility mechanically and does not characterize rapid central neural timing precision.
Visual spatial acuity belongs to the visual system rather than describing auditory gap detection and temporal tracking.
Correct. Temporal resolution contributes to processing rapidly changing speech and environmental sounds and is distinct from threshold sensitivity.

items.prompt: What is the preferred first step in a hierarchy of controls for hazardous noise?
choices: Eliminate or reduce noise at its source through engineering changes before relying solely on earplugs.
Distribute disposable foam earplugs across the floor right away without measuring or modifying noisy machines.
Shorten annual workplace hearing screening protocols so employees return to loud workstations more quickly.
Wait until serial audiograms confirm permanent threshold shifts before recommending workplace noise abatement.
items.rationale: Source and engineering controls reduce exposure broadly; administrative controls and well-fitted protection supplement rather than replace them.
choiceRationales: Correct. Source and engineering controls reduce exposure broadly; administrative controls and well-fitted protection supplement rather than replace them.
Personal hearing protection sits lower in the hierarchy of controls and depends on consistent fit compared with source reduction.
Shortening hearing tests reduces surveillance quality and does nothing to lower hazardous workplace occupational acoustic exposure.
Waiting for permanent threshold shift accepts preventable cochlear damage instead of applying proactive engineering noise prevention.

items.prompt: What does a comprehensive hearing-conservation program include?
choices: Annual pure-tone monitoring conducted routinely without implementing workplace noise controls or training.
Exposure surveys, engineering and work controls, fitted protection, training, audiometry, and follow-up.
Bulk distribution of single-size hearing protectors in break rooms without fit verification or staff education.
Individual audiologic counseling offered after employees develop severe permanent noise-induced hearing loss.
items.rationale: Conservation requires coordinated prevention, monitoring, education, protection, and timely response under current occupational rules.
choiceRationales: Monitoring detects threshold shifts after exposure occurs yet cannot prevent noise damage without hazard controls and education.
Correct. Conservation requires coordinated prevention, monitoring, education, protection, and timely response under current occupational rules.
Handing out unverified protectors frequently yields poor real-world attenuation and leaves workers unprotected in hazardous noise.
Waiting for severe loss turns prevention into late rehabilitation rather than protecting workers across the full conservation cycle.

items.prompt: What is the purpose of ototoxicity monitoring?
choices: Ensure that the prescribing physician halts the potentially ototoxic medication immediately upon any shift.
Diagnose systemic renal or neurological medication side effects independently during audiology appointments.
Detect clinically meaningful auditory change early to inform medical discussion, communication support, and follow-up.
Replace ongoing physician and oncology treatment management with audiology-directed dosing adjustments.
items.rationale: Ototoxic monitoring documents change using sensitive, repeatable methods and communicates results to the authorized medical team and patient.
choiceRationales: Medical teams weigh lifesaving treatment benefits against hearing risks; audiology informs shared medical decisions rather than guaranteeing stoppage.
Systemic medical side effects fall outside audiologic scope and require physician assessment rather than independent audiologic diagnosis.
Correct. Ototoxic monitoring documents change using sensitive, repeatable methods and communicates results to the authorized medical team and patient.
Medication dosing remains the prescribing physician’s decision, supported collaboratively by timely audiologic baseline and serial data.

items.prompt: How should hearing protection be selected?
choices: Issue the highest labeled attenuation protector to every employee so maximum noise reduction applies universally.
Purchase one universal earplug style assuming standard canal sizes fit workers across the facility comfortably.
Use personal hearing protection in place of evaluating excessive noise levels or feasible engineering controls.
Match attenuation, fit, comfort, communication needs, gear compatibility, and measured exposure, then verify use.
items.rationale: Over- or underprotection, poor fit, inconsistent use, and communication demands affect real-world protection and safety.
choiceRationales: Over-attenuation can block warning signals and coworker speech, prompting workers to remove protectors in variable noise.
Ear-canal anatomy varies widely; one size often causes discomfort or poor seal, requiring individualized fit verification.
Personal protection complements rather than replaces exposure measurement and higher-tier engineering workplace source noise control reductions.
Correct. Over- or underprotection, poor fit, inconsistent use, and communication demands affect real-world protection and safety.

items.prompt: Which counseling message best supports recreational hearing safety?
choices: Manage level, duration, distance, recovery, monitoring, and fitted protection while preserving music goals.
Advise that every sound exposure carries identical cochlear hazard regardless of intensity level or duration.
Reassure musicians that brief post-concert ringing or dullness can be disregarded once quiet returns.
Explain that only industrial occupational noise damages hearing while recreational music remains benign.
items.rationale: Risk reflects exposure level, duration, spectrum, susceptibility, recovery, and repeated dose; individualized harm reduction supports adherence.
choiceRationales: Correct. Risk reflects exposure level, duration, spectrum, susceptibility, recovery, and repeated dose; individualized harm reduction supports adherence.
Noise risk depends critically on both intensity and exposure duration, so reducing level, time, or proximity cuts risk.
Temporary tinnitus or threshold shift is an early warning sign of acoustic stress that warrants protective changes.
The cochlea responds to acoustic energy regardless of source, so high-level recreational music poses real hearing-loss risk.

items.prompt: What does a hearing screening result establish?
choices: The failed screening result confirms permanent sensorineural hearing loss in the tested classroom ear.
The child needs timely follow-up; screening alone cannot diagnose hearing-loss type, degree, or cause.
The screening result establishes that the student requires immediate fitting with personal amplification.
No clinical follow-up is necessary unless the teacher notices severe academic delays later in the term.
items.rationale: Screening identifies risk under defined conditions and requires clear referral, tracking, and diagnostic follow-up. This response best integrates audiologic evidence, the referral purpose, person and family priorities, safety, access, professional scope, and appropriate follow-up.
choiceRationales: A screen identifies possible risk only and cannot distinguish transient fluid, wax, room noise, or permanent sensorineural loss.

Correct. Screening identifies risk under defined conditions and requires clear referral, tracking, and diagnostic follow-up. This response best integrates audiologic evidence, the referral purpose, person and family priorities, safety, access, professional scope, and appropriate follow-up.
Amplification requires a full diagnostic audiologic evaluation and medical clearance rather than a single screening refer.
Unaddressed hearing differences can affect classroom access and speech perception early, making timely diagnostic follow-up essential.

items.prompt: Why do newborn programs use OAE and/or automated ABR technologies?
choices: They directly measure early receptive language comprehension and emergent phonetic speech recognition.
They determine exact prescriptive hearing-aid gain targets across speech frequencies for immediate fitting.
They estimate physiologic auditory-system responses without requiring a conditioned behavioral response.
They eliminate the need for diagnostic audiologic evaluation whenever an infant receives a refer outcome.
items.rationale: Physiologic screening supports early identification, but pass or refer outcomes remain screening results and risk factors can require surveillance.
choiceRationales: OAE and automated ABR assess peripheral cochlear or neural pathway integrity rather than cognitive language comprehension.
Screening pass/refer outputs do not yield frequency-specific thresholds needed to prescribe or verify hearing-aid amplification settings.
Correct. Physiologic screening supports early identification, but pass or refer outcomes remain screening results and risk factors can require surveillance.
Newborn screening identifies infants needing prompt diagnostic testing rather than replacing comprehensive follow-up audiologic diagnostic confirmation.

items.prompt: What should happen after an infant does not pass a rescreen?
choices: Wait until the toddler shows observable speech or vocabulary delays before scheduling diagnostic audiology.
Fit bilateral hearing aids right away based on the failed newborn screen so auditory stimulation begins early.
Assume transient middle-ear fluid explains the refer result and schedule another routine screening next year.
Arrange prompt diagnostic audiologic evaluation and coordinated EHDI follow-up instead of endless rescreening.
items.rationale: Timely diagnostic evaluation reduces loss to follow-up and supports informed family-centered intervention when indicated.
choiceRationales: Waiting for spoken-language delay sacrifices critical early neurodevelopmental windows that national EHDI timelines aim to protect.
Safe, accurate amplification requires confirmed frequency-specific diagnostic thresholds and physician medical clearance before infant hearing-device fitting.
Repeating screens indefinitely or assuming fluid risks missing permanent hearing loss or auditory neuropathy spectrum disorder.
Correct. Timely diagnostic evaluation reduces loss to follow-up and supports informed family-centered intervention when indicated.

items.prompt: Which condition is essential for valid school pure-tone screening?
choices: Verify equipment calibration and ambient-noise limits and modify or relocate testing before interpreting data.
Raise every pure-tone screening intensity level informally without documentation so tones cut through room noise.
Record students tested in the noisy room as passing to prevent inflating unnecessary clinic referral rates.
Proceed unchanged because standard supra-aural screening headphones block low-frequency ambient room noise fully.
items.rationale: Ambient noise can mask screening signals and increase false referrals; quality control is essential. This response best integrates audiologic evidence, the referral purpose, person and family priorities, safety, access, professional scope, and appropriate follow-up.
choiceRationales: Correct. Ambient noise can mask screening signals and increase false referrals; quality control is essential. This response best integrates audiologic evidence, the referral purpose, person and family priorities, safety, access, professional scope, and appropriate follow-up.
Raising screening levels informally invalidates protocol cutoffs and risks missing genuine mild or low-frequency hearing loss.
Marking unverified screens as passing conceals real hearing barriers and defeats the purpose of school identification.
Supra-aural headphones provide limited low-frequency attenuation, so excessive low-frequency ambient room noise causes frequent false-positive fails.

items.prompt: An infant passed newborn hearing screening, but later develops caregiver concerns and a risk factor associated with delayed-onset change. What is the appropriate next step?
choices: Treat the original pass as conclusive regardless of the current concern or documented risk.
Arrange age-appropriate audiologic surveillance or evaluation based on the current concern and risk.
Wait for a confirmed language delay before gathering additional auditory information.
Repeat newborn screening indefinitely instead of obtaining age-appropriate diagnostic data.
items.rationale: A newborn screening pass describes hearing-screen status at one time and does not rule out progressive, delayed-onset, or subsequently acquired change. New caregiver concern or a recognized risk indicator warrants age-appropriate surveillance or comprehensive evaluation under the current EHDI and clinical pathway.
choiceRationales: Not the best answer. A prior pass does not override a new functional concern or risk indicator because auditory status can change after the newborn period.
Correct. Current concern and delayed-onset risk call for developmentally appropriate surveillance or diagnostic evaluation rather than reliance on the earlier screen.
Not the best answer. Waiting for a confirmed language delay can postpone identification; hearing status should be evaluated when a relevant concern or risk emerges.
Not the best answer. Repeating an infant screening protocol indefinitely does not provide the age-appropriate diagnostic information needed to resolve current concern.

items.prompt: What is the main purpose of comparing air- and bone-conduction thresholds?
choices: To diagnose an expressive language disorder independently during a routine audiologic appointment.
To quantify vestibulo-ocular reflex gain across rapid head-impulse balance movements accurately.
To differentiate conductive, sensorineural, and mixed components of a patient’s hearing loss.
To verify real-ear hearing-aid output targets inside the ear canal across soft and loud speech.

Use bone-conduction pure-tone thresholds as the primary outcome measure for everyday noisy communication.

An objective electrophysiologic test recording brainstem potentials while the preschooler sleeps quietly.
An acoustic immittance procedure assessing tympanic-membrane mobility and middle-ear static air pressure.

Close agreement between the obtained pure-tone pattern and the referring physician’s tentative diagnostic note.

items.prompt: A flat tympanogram with normal ear-canal volume is commonly associated with what?
choices: Markedly reduced middle-ear mobility such as effusion, confirmed through the complete evaluation.

items.prompt: What do present otoacoustic emissions indicate?

The speed of central vestibular balance compensation following unilateral peripheral canal injury.

As an objective proxy needing protocol-specific correction and behavioral confirmation later.

Unsupervised vestibular exercises are unsafe during an undiagnosed acute neurologic event requiring urgent immediate medical evaluation.

Treat every report of sound intolerance as the identical clinical condition requiring one fixed sound protocol.

items.prompt: Which pattern supports conductive hearing loss?

An isolated central auditory brainstem processing disorder with intact peripheral thresholds.

A nonauditory vestibular disorder that leaves air- and bone-conduction thresholds unrelated.

Correct. Elevated bone-conduction thresholds indicate a sensorineural component, while additional, repeatable air–bone gaps indicate a conductive component. With appropriate masking and cross-checks, the combined configuration is classified as mixed rather than purely conductive or purely sensorineural.

Assume impacted earwax explains the rapid drop without performing otoscopy or medical referral.

Amplification cannot substitute for urgent medical assessment and potential time-critical medical treatment of sudden hearing loss.

An isolated conductive middle-ear effusion with normal retrocochlear neural timing and synchrony.

items.prompt: What should an educational audiology assessment address beyond thresholds?

items.prompt: How should a multidisciplinary team interpret listening difficulty with normal peripheral hearing?
